name: Zoe Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zoe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on my husband's family farm, which his dad Frank still runs. It's oats and oilseed rape on the better ground and four hundred ewes on the hill, plus a little shop at the gate where we sell lamb boxes. Frank pays me a wage, not a big one, and Dan works off the farm as an electrician, which is lucky, because his money is what keeps the bungalow mortgage paid.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at six, checked the ewes on the quad bike, then spent two hours sorting lambs for the lamb boxes with the dog, Bess. Afternoon was the lambing records and the tax forms, which I hate, so I got one of those AI chat apps to explain a form to me, and it actually helped. Then the school run, because Ruby's fifteen and has a dentist appointment every other week, it feels like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's sensible, I never thought it would take over farming. It's handy for forms and that's about it. I'd probably say that in the farm shop when someone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means we carry on as we are. Frank still makes the big decisions, I still do the sheep and the paperwork, and money stays tight. I'd be quietly glad not to have to learn anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same plan as now: try to get the lamb boxes up from twenty a month to thirty, and keep using the chat app for forms. I'd ask Frank for a small pay rise in the spring, like I do every year, and he'd say 'next year'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little bored by it, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why thirty lamb boxes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At thirty a month the shop pays for itself and a bit more, and that bit more could be my pay rise. I did the sums with Dan one Sunday. He's better at numbers than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's it like working for your father-in-law?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. He's fair but he's slow to change anything, he still wants the lambing book on paper. I've learned to suggest things twice, a month apart, and the second time he thinks it was his idea.

S0.say: It's sensible that AI didn't take over farming, since it's handy for forms and little else. She'd say that in the farm shop if someone asked.
S0.think: The farm carries on as before: her father-in-law makes the big decisions, she runs the sheep and paperwork, and money stays tight. She's quietly glad not to have to learn anything big.
S0.do: Keeps working towards thirty lamb boxes a month from twenty, and uses the chat app for forms. Asks her father-in-law for a small spring pay rise, as she does every year.
S0.quote: I've learned to suggest things twice, a month apart, and the second time he thinks it was his idea.
S0.fieldNote: She is measured and practical, with a clear target for the farm shop. The family dynamic with her father-in-law shapes everything she can change. Her trick for getting ideas past him shows patience rather than resistance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to look at what works and use it, and not get carried away. Farms have always changed, my granddad didn't have a quad bike. I'd be the one saying 'let's see a farm that's tried it first'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit uneasy, because the paperwork part of my job is the bit AI does best. If the AI does the records and the tax, what am I paid for? The sheep, I suppose, until there's a robot dog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to a demonstration day at the agricultural college and see the kit working on a real farm. I'd learn the record-keeping software properly so it's me running it, not replacing me. And I'd push the lamb boxes harder, because selling to people face to face is something I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but I'd notice myself thinking about it while I'm on the quad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Frank buy any of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not until the neighbour has, and the neighbour's son has, and it's half price. That's both a problem and a comfort. It gives me time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Dan think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He thinks it's good for him, there'd be more wiring and installing work. He'd say 'you'll be fine, Zo'. He doesn't see that if the farm needs less of me, Frank would quietly stop paying me.

S1.say: It's sensible to use what works without getting carried away, since farms have always changed. She'd want to see a farm that's tried it first.
S1.think: She's uneasy because paperwork, which AI does best, is a big part of her job. If AI does the records and tax, she wonders what she's paid for besides the sheep.
S1.do: Goes to a demonstration day at the agricultural college to see the equipment working on a real farm. Learns the record-keeping software properly so she runs it, and pushes the lamb box sales.
S1.feel: Uneasy, not losing sleep but thinking about it on the quad bike.
S1.quote: He doesn't see that if the farm needs less of me, Frank would quietly stop paying me.
S1.fieldNote: Her position in a family business makes her job less secure than it looks: her wage depends on her father-in-law's goodwill. She sees her husband's optimism as missing the point. Her slow-moving father-in-law is both a risk and a buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a sensible plan from the government, quickly, and I'd want to see it before anyone panics. Not a ban, not a free-for-all. Just help for people while things settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the sheep go to robots and the shop goes online run by an AI, and Frank either sells up or keeps it as a hobby. Two years is about the time it takes to get a flock bred the way you want it. That's how short it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut what we can straight away: Ruby's riding lessons, the second car. I'd look for work off the farm, maybe in the vet's office or a school, while there's still anything with people in it. And I'd ask Frank to keep me on part-time for the lamb boxes, because people still like buying from a face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops just picturing telling Ruby the riding's stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would riding be first to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's ninety a month and it's the one thing that isn't food or the house. Leo plays football, which is free. It's not fair on Ruby, but that's how the sums come out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Dan thinks the change is good for him. Does that hold in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a year, maybe, he'd be busy wiring robots into barns. After that the robots wire themselves, I suppose. So I'd tell him to save every penny of that year.

S2.say: She'd want a sensible government plan quickly, before anyone panics. Not a ban or a free-for-all, just help for people while things settle.
S2.think: She expects robots to take the sheep, an AI to run the shop online, and her father-in-law to sell up or farm as a hobby. Two years is about the time it takes to breed a flock the way you want it.
S2.do: Cuts her daughter's riding lessons and the second car straight away and looks for off-farm work at the vet's office or a school. Asks her father-in-law to keep her part-time for the lamb boxes and tells her husband to save his extra wiring income.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with her stomach dropping at the thought of stopping her daughter's riding.
S2.quote: Two years is about the time it takes to get a flock bred the way you want it. That's how short it is.
S2.fieldNote: She measures the timeline against breeding a flock, which makes the speed vivid. Her cuts are planned in order, starting with the riding lessons, and she's openly uncomfortable about the fairness. She sees her husband's short-term boom as something to save, not spend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for sensible planning, and I'd want the farming groups and the government talking now. I'd say farm families need help changing, not just the big companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough for me to get into something else before the farm stops needing me. I wouldn't wait for Frank. I'd be forty-eight, which isn't too old to start something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look at a part-time course, maybe as a veterinary nurse, or teaching assistant, something with people or animals in the room. I'd keep doing the sheep while I study. And we'd try to put a little away each month, even if it's just Dan's overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can manage. It's like the run-up to lambing, you know it's coming and you get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of those two would you pick?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Veterinary nurse, if I'm honest, because I've done more for ewes than most vet nurses ever will. But it's a two-year course and I'd need to find the fees. Teaching assistant is quicker and cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to help you study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I already use it to explain the tax forms, so I'd use it to explain anatomy. Ruby says it's cheating. I'd tell her it's a tutor I can't afford otherwise.

S3.say: Five years is enough time for sensible planning, and farming groups and government should start talking now. Farm families need help changing, not just big companies.
S3.think: Five years is enough to move into something else before the farm stops needing her, without waiting for her father-in-law. At 48 she wouldn't be too old to start something new.
S3.do: Starts a part-time course as a veterinary nurse or teaching assistant in the first year while still doing the sheep. Uses AI as a study helper and saves Dan's overtime each month.
S3.feel: Anxious but manageable, like the run-up to lambing.
S3.quote: I'd tell her it's a tutor I can't afford otherwise.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she plans to leave the farm on her own terms rather than wait for her father-in-law. She weighs two courses on cost and time, which shows careful thinking. She uses AI comfortably for learning even though she doesn't seek it out otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a sensible amount of time, so let's not waste it arguing. Train people, help the farms that want to change, and let the old ones retire with some dignity. Like Frank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I'd be fine if I start soon. Ruby and Leo would be grown up. Frank would be eighty, and the farm would probably go to robots or get rented out, and Dan and I would need to decide about the bungalow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the vet nurse course over two years, part-time, and keep the lamb boxes going as a side thing. I'd talk to Frank properly about what happens to the farm, which nobody in the family wants to do. And we'd help Ruby choose something to study that will still be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but mostly okay. Ten years is long enough to get used to anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does nobody want to talk to Frank about the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it means talking about him dying, and because Dan's brother thinks he's getting the land. It's a family thing. AI might be what finally makes us have the conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ruby to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She wants to be a vet, actually, which is funny. I'd tell her to go for it, because a robot can do a lot, but I'd still want a person telling me my dog's going to die.

S4.say: Ten years is sensible time, so it shouldn't be wasted arguing. Train people, help farms that want to change and let older farmers like Frank retire with dignity.
S4.think: She'd be fine if she starts soon, with her children grown by the time it lands. The farm would probably go to robots or be rented out, and the family would need to decide about the bungalow.
S4.do: Takes the veterinary nurse course part-time over two years and keeps the lamb boxes as a side income. Raises the farm's future with her father-in-law and helps her daughter choose a lasting field of study.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly okay, since ten years is long enough to get used to anything.
S4.quote: I'd still want a person telling me my dog's going to die.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years the scenario becomes a family planning problem as much as a work one. She expects AI to force a long-avoided conversation about who inherits the farm. Her support for her daughter's vet ambition mirrors her own course choice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years isn't enough for Frank to decide anything, never mind me. What would help is support for part-time courses for people like me, and some income while you're doing them, so you don't have to pick between the course and the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the dog. Bess is nine and she's the best worker on the farm. If robots herd the sheep, she'd be out of a job before me, and that sounds silly, but it's what I'd think about first.

headlineQuote: If robots herd the sheep, she'd be out of a job before me, and that sounds silly, but it's what I'd think about first.
portrait: Zoe Lopez is 43 and works for a modest wage on her father-in-law Frank's sheep and arable farm, running the flock, the paperwork and a gate shop selling lamb boxes, while her husband Dan's electrician wage covers the mortgage. She is practical and middle-of-the-road, uses AI tools now and then for forms, and likes to see a change working before she tries it. She is calm when AI fizzles and uneasy with steady change, because the paperwork side of her job is easy to automate. With AGI in two years she is alarmed and cuts her daughter's riding lessons. With more time she plans to retrain as a veterinary nurse and finally face the family conversation about the farm's future.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because two years isn't enough time for her father-in-law to decide anything, let alone for her to change course.
whatWouldHelp: Support for part-time courses and some income while doing them, so she doesn't have to choose between studying and paying the mortgage.
